## Proof

Place the center of the circular laboratory floor at the origin. The two rectangles are centered at the origin and oriented perpendicularly.

**Rectangle 1** (horizontal): 24 m along the $x$-axis, 10 m along the $y$-axis. Its four corners are
$$(\pm 12,\ \pm 5).$$

**Rectangle 2** (vertical): 10 m along the $x$-axis, 24 m along the $y$-axis. Its four corners are
$$(\pm 5,\ \pm 12).$$

**Finding the circle.** All eight corners lie on the circular boundary. The distance of corner $(12,5)$ from the origin is
$$\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=\sqrt{144+25}=\sqrt{169}=13.$$
The distance of corner $(5,12)$ from the origin is
$$\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=\sqrt{25+144}=\sqrt{169}=13.$$
By symmetry all eight corners have the same distance $13$ from the origin, so they lie on a common circle of radius $R=13$ centered at the origin. This is consistent: a single circle passes through all eight corners.

**Area of the circular floor.**
$$A_{\text{circle}}=\pi R^2=169\pi.$$

**Area of the two arrays (union).** Each rectangle has area $10\times 24=240$, so the two together cover
$$2\times 240=480$$
before accounting for overlap. The two rectangles cross perpendicularly at their centers. Their intersection is the region satisfying both
$$|x|\le 12,\ |y|\le 5 \quad\text{and}\quad |x|\le 5,\ |y|\le 12,$$
which reduces to
$$|x|\le 5,\ |y|\le 5.$$
This is a $10\times 10$ square of area $100$.

By inclusion–exclusion, the total area covered by the arrays is
$$A_{\text{arrays}}=480-100=380.$$

**Gray-tiled area.** The gray tile covers the part of the circular floor not occupied by the arrays:
$$A_{\text{gray}}=A_{\text{circle}}-A_{\text{arrays}}=169\pi-380.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
